  Francesca McCaffen and Sean McCaffen spoke on behalf of The Children’s
  Lifesaving Foundation and explained that the funds would be used for underserved
  kids and programs such as the counselor-in-training program.

  Jennifer Brent spoke on behalf of the California Wildlife Center and described the
  rescue, rehab, and release procedures in the City of Malibu. She stated that they
  educate the community and gather data for future use.

  Joel Schulman spoke on behalf of Poison Free Malibu. He spoke regarding
  education efforts including an education campaign, yard signs, posters, t-shirts,
  signs, and a coloring book.

  Denise de Garmo spoke on behalf of the Malibu Foundation. She thanked the
  subcommittee for their donation last year and is requesting funds this year for
  education outreach and a community native nursery and shrubbery.

  Dawn Ericson spoke on behalf of the Beach Ecology Coalition. She stated that the
  funding would benefit the Junior Lifeguard program via a seashore guide that
  would be distributed to 4,000 junior lifeguards.

  Georgia spoke on behalf of the Malibu Monarch Project. She stated that they have
  a goal of increasing biodiversity. She also added that there are goals to create an
  education poster and flashcards for schools.

  Ellen Shane spoke on behalf of the Emily Shane Foundation. She thanked the city
  for being a great partner. She stated that funding would benefit kids who struggle
  in school via individualized tutoring and mentoring.

  Keegan Gibbs from the LA Emergency Preparedness Foundation (Community
  Brigades) spoke in favor of a partnership with the city and spoke about the multi-
  stakeholder approach. He spoke about the importance of the program.

  John Mazza spoke on behalf of the Adamson House. He spoke about the junior
  ranger program, K-12 bus transportation funds, and the need for funding for
  operational costs due to sea lice and leaks.

  Kasey Earnest spoke on behalf of the Boys and Girls Club of Malibu. She spoke
  about the kid's efforts to address mental health, providing resources to the aging
  population, and the goal to fill in service gaps.

  Lisa Saila spoke on behalf of the Aurelia Foundation and Hand in Hand. She stated
  that the Aurelia Foundation has the goal of engaging people with disabilities in the
  community where funds would go to transportation costs into Malibu. She also
  stated that Hand in Hand is a social integration club for people with disabilities.

  Neal Thornhill spoke on behalf of the Malibu Search and Rescue. He stated that
  coverage includes the Santa Monica Mountains and is covered by volunteers. He
  added that funding would be for volunteer equipment.

  Councilmember Silverstein inquired about state funding of the program.

  Mr. Thornhill stated that historically they have not received funding. He stated that
  in this location they are the most busy out of all of the state and receive 2-3 calls
  per week.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about financial support from other cities and the
  number of calls in Malibu.

  Mr. Thornhill stated that the City of Agoura provides about $1000 - $3000 and
  added that about 50% of the calls come from the coast and there may be some
  overlap due to trails that go into unincorporated county.

  Richard Fink spoke on behalf of the California State Parks. He stated that they have
  20 million annual visitors primarily in Malibu Lagoon, Adamson House, and local
  beaches. He stated that funds would go towards Malibu improvements such as
  archival or materials and infrastructure updates to improve the visitor experience.
  He stated that the agency is committed to implementing poison-free efforts in
  Malibu.

  Councilmember Silverstein inquired if this was a request on behalf of the state or a
  nonprofit division of the state.

  Mr. Fink stated that this request is on behalf of a division of the state.

  Talley Hutcherson of the Cavallo Foundation Malibu spoke about the programs
  offered in Malibu aimed at improving mental health at the Malibu Equestrian Park.

  Max Gorby spoke on behalf of the Malibu Scouts Troop 224, spoke about the
  impacts of the programs on kids, and added that many of the kids come from
  middle-income families, and requested funding to impact more kids.

  Councilmember Silverstein requested additional details about their budget.

  Mr. Gorby stated that the budget is scalable and can work with various levels of
  funding, he specified that they are currently supporting 15 kids.

  Chris Baca from Meals on Wheels spoke about the program’s efforts in Malibu. He
  shared that there was a growth of need for services in Malibu and that they provide
  resources beyond meals to those in need.

  Councilmember Silverstein inquired about the housing status of those served in
  Malibu.

  Mr. Baca stated that they provide services to people in their homes.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about other government funding for these
  services.

  Mr. Baca stated that only 20% of funding comes from government agencies.

  Scott Hosfeld with Malibu Friends of Music spoke about their musical resources
  such as training. He spoke about making musical resources accessible.

  Julia Forth spoke on behalf of Cancer Support Los Angeles, she stated that they
  provide free mental health services that can be provided online.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about the number of people served in Malibu.

  Ms. Forth stated that they serve an estimated 100 people in Malibu.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart closed public comment.

  Councilmember Silverstein provided general comments regarding the applications
  he read, he commended the applicants for their work and pointed to the limited
  funds available. He explained his decision-making process, including favoring
  programs for organizations serving in Malibu. Inquired about a government agency
  funding a religious corporation. He added that it is difficult when groups ask for a
  large amount of funds in proportion to what is available to give.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart explained that they are subject to the Brown Act and that
  they have not gotten a chance to discuss this beforehand. He explained that
  $575,000 was requested and they can only allocate $200,000. He reiterated his
  desire to see Malibu-centric efforts. He explained that applicants associated with
  religious groups, in the past, if the resources weren’t used on religious efforts, the
  community allocation was appropriate. He inquired regarding the possibility of
  increasing the budget for this fund by $25,000.

  City Manager McClary shared that it would be a good question for the City Council.
  He also added that applications were accepted so long as they are a nonprofit
  organization and show that the program was open for the general public.

  Councilmember Silverstein stated that because a budget workshop and a previous
  Administration and Finance Committee was held, he recommends keeping the
  budget at $200,000 for this item. He explained that if applicants do not get what
  was desired there are other opportunities to receive funding from the city. He
  explained that he does not agree with the city providing funding to the state.

  B. Fiscal Year 2023-24 Third Quarter Financial Report

  Recommended Action: Review Fiscal Year (FY) 2023-24 Third Quarter Financial
  Report.

  Assistant City Manager Toney presented the staff report. He provided a high-level
  summary which included revenues and expenditures. He stated that the third quarter
  is similar to the third quarter of the previous year.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about property taxes.

  Assistant City Manager Toney clarified that projecting property tax payments are
  not split in half and explained that one payment is larger than the other and other
  smaller payment disbursements.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about the FEMA reimbursement.

  Assistant City Manager Toney stated that the process could take longer than
  expected and depends on how projects are closed.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about the interest earnings, wastewater, and park
  development totals.

  Assistant City Manager Toney stated that he would follow up on getting an answer
  regarding these totals.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about the available SCE funds.

  Assistant City Manager Toney stated that those funds are still tied to some projects
  and shared that they can get additional information on how these funds were
  allocated.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about the budget for Public Safety.

  Assistant City Manager Toney stated that a large portion of those funds are for the
  Sheriff Substation, however, added that hiring has been difficult, and they have
  lowered those appropriations for the upcoming fiscal year.

  Councilmember Silverstein inquired about personnel being a line item and inquired
  if it could be added to the quarterly reports.

  Finance Manager Neermann stated that personnel is a line item in the budget, and
  shared that personnel could be added as a separate schedule in the quarterly reports

  as a total. She stated that it would take effort to include this information for each
  department, but the department would do what they can.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about capital project spending.

  Assistant City Manager Toney stated that some of the lack of spending is due to
  multi-year projects getting full allocation.

  Finance Manager Neermann agreed and shared that they have spoken with the
  departments and have asked them to only add to the budget what is anticipated for
  the one year instead of allocating the funds for a multiyear project.

  City Manager McClary shared that in working with neighboring cities he has
  learned that this is a common issue amongst other cities. He stated that there is also
  a built-in lag where payments aren’t paid until later in the fiscal year.

  Assistant City Manager Toney reiterated the importance of a 5-year plan for capital
  improvement plans and grant funding.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about the Legacy Park debt service.

  Finance Manager Neermann stated that the city receives a one-time annual invoice.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart inquired about surplus funds.

  Assistant City Manager Toney stated that there are many reasons, including a lack
  of staffing and creating better department projections.

Subject:  Appropriation of Funds in the Amount of $460,000 from the Office of
  Traffic Safety Grant (Reimbursement Grant)

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Provide a recommendation to the City Council concerning
the appropriation of funds in the amount of $460,000 from the Office of Traffic Safety Grant
(Reimbursement Grant).

FISCAL IMPACT: Funding for this initiative was not included in the Adopted Budget for
FY 2024-2025. The total appropriation requested is $460,000, which will be used for
enforcement, education, and outreach activities as outlined below. There is no direct
impact on the City’s General Fund. This is a reimbursement grant, meaning the City of
Malibu will front the costs associated with these traffic safety initiatives, with
reimbursement provided by the Office of Traffic Safety upon submission of qualifying
expenses.

STRATEGIC PRIORITY: This item is not part of the Adopted Strategic Work Plan for FY
23-24.

DISCUSSION: The City of Malibu has been awarded a reimbursement grant in the amount
of $460,000 from the Office of Traffic Safety (OTS) to support a variety of traffic safety
initiatives, including enforcement operations and public safety education. Under the terms
of the grant, the City is required to initially cover expenses for the activities, with
reimbursement provided by the OTS upon receipt of proper documentation.

The grant funds are proposed to be used to facilitate DUI checkpoints, saturation patrols,
general traffic enforcement, and educational campaigns aimed at reducing impaired
driving and promoting road safety over the next federal fiscal year.

  Page 1 of 3
  Item # 3.B.
 The total grant allocation of $460,000 is recommended to be distributed across three key
areas: enforcement, public education, and outreach, as outlined below.

1. DUI Checkpoints and Saturation Operations
Over the next fiscal year, the City plans to conduct four (4) DUI checkpoints and eight (8)
saturation operations. These operations will focus on general traffic enforcement and DUI
prevention.

Quarterly Plan:
  • One (1) DUI checkpoint
  • Two (2) saturation operations (1 DUI-focused and 1 general traffic enforcement)

The total cost for these enforcement operations is $86,528. To account for any potential
mid-year salary increases, a 5% Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) has been applied,
bringing the total estimated cost to $90,960.

The breakdown is as follows:
  • DUI Enforcement: $76,260
  • General Traffic Enforcement: $14,700

2. Malibu – Surf, Sand, Slow Educational Campaign (Contractual Services)

The City has engaged That’s Sound! Productions (TTS!) to execute the "Malibu – Surf,
Sand, Slow" educational campaign, a key component of our public safety outreach. This
initiative focuses on educating the public about traffic safety, including impaired driving
and general road safety awareness. TTS! will be responsible for producing and delivering
educational materials, services, and experiential events designed to enhance traffic safety
awareness. The "21 Miles in Malibu" experiential events are a central part of this
campaign. TTS! will provide regular progress reports, event coordination, and
communication materials to ensure compliance with the City's requirements and OTS
guidelines.

Cost Breakdown for Campaign:
  • General Traffic Education: $185,300
  • Drinking & Driving Education: $139,700

The total cost for this campaign is $325,000.

3. Remaining Funds: Expansion of Enforcement Operations
After the allocations for enforcement and educational initiatives, there is a remaining
balance of $44,040.. Staff proposes that these funds be used to expand DUI and general
traffic enforcement operations within the City of Malibu, as resources and staff availability
allow.

  Item # 3.B.
 Proposed Use of Remaining Funds:
  • Expand enforcement operations, such as additional DUI checkpoints and saturation
  patrols
  • Ensure flexibility for enhanced traffic safety enforcement efforts in response to
  community needs
